title: November 9: A Day of Remembrance, Reflection, and Responsibility
author: Todd Polikoff, Chief Executive Officer, Aaron Family JCC
body:
Today, November 9, marks two moments that changed modern history. They happened 51 years apart, yet together they teach us something about the choices societies make and the responsibility we share for what comes next.

On November 9, 1938, Nazi Germany unleashed Kristallnacht, the Night of Broken Glass. Across Germany and Austria, mobs attacked and burned Jewish homes, businesses, and synagogues. Jewish men were beaten, and thousands were sent to concentration camps. Countless families learned, in a single night, that their own country had turned against them.

Yet Kristallnacht did not happen overnight; it followed years of economic hardship, extreme nationalism, conspiracy theories, and scapegoating that made antisemitism seem normal. Long before the windows were shattered, Jewish citizens had been stripped of their rights, shut out of public life, and painted as enemies of their own nation. Too many people stayed silent or told themselves it was not their concern.

On the same date in 1989, the Berlin Wall opened. For 28 years, it had divided families and an entire city. Its opening showed the world that division can be overcome and freedom restored.

These anniversaries are not equal in their history or their human cost. Still, sharing a date invites reflection. One shows us what happens when hatred becomes acceptable; the other shows us that walls, even ones that seem permanent, can come down when people find the courage to challenge them.

Kristallnacht teaches us that we must not wait for hatred to turn violent before recognizing its significance. Bigotry is never excusable, even when directed at someone whose views we oppose. Every person's dignity and safety must be protected, regardless of their politics, faith, or place of origin.

At The J, we believe community is built through connection. We are here to create a place where people belong, where our children learn respect, and where people of different backgrounds come together around shared values. That work has never mattered more.

We cannot control every force shaping our society, but we can shape the community we build together. We can stand against antisemitism and every form of hatred. We can show respect even when we disagree, and we can bring people together rather than let them retreat behind the divisions that define so much of our world.

Remembrance carries responsibility. We must never accept hatred as normal, and we must never stop working toward a world where the walls between us come down.

That is the work of the J, and it is a responsibility we all share.

Todd

title: Parshat Chayei Sarah and Veterans Day: The Legacy We Carry
author: Todd Polikoff, Chief Executive Officer, Aaron Family JCC
body:
This Shabbat, as we read Parashat Chayei Sarah, we encounter a portion of the Torah that begins with Sarah's death. Yet, despite its title, “The Life of Sarah,” much of the portion is about what happens after her passing. Abraham mourns his wife, honors her memory, and begins thinking about their family's future. Her life may have ended, but her influence and legacy would continue through the generations that followed.

This week's Torah portion connects meaningfully to Veterans Day, which we will observe on November 11. We honor the men and women who have served our country not simply for the years they wore a uniform, but for the sacrifices they made and the lasting impact of their service. Their legacy lives on in the freedoms we enjoy, the opportunities available to future generations, and the communities we have the privilege of building.

Both Chayei Sarah and Veterans Day remind us that a person's life is measured not only by the years they lived or the work they accomplished, but also by what they leave behind. Legacy is not simply about remembering the past; it is about recognizing how the actions and sacrifices of those who came before us shape our present and influence our future.

At the Aaron Family JCC, we see the importance of that legacy every day. We bring generations together, create opportunities for meaningful connections, and help pass along the traditions, values, and relationships that strengthen our community. The work we do today becomes part of the foundation future generations will build on.

As we approach Veterans Day, let us take a moment to thank those who have served our country and recognize the families who have shared in their sacrifices. May we honor their legacy not only through our gratitude, but through the way we live, the communities we strengthen, and the opportunities we create for those who will follow us.

Shabbat Shalom,

Todd

title: Room for One More: Abraham’s Tent and Israel’s Democracy
author: Todd Polikoff, Chief Executive Officer, Aaron Family JCC
body:
Aaron Family JCC Community,

This week’s Torah portion, Parshat Vayera, opens with Abraham sitting at the entrance of his tent as three strangers approach. Despite the heat, he rushes to greet them, offers food and rest, and makes them feel welcome. Jewish tradition holds up this moment as an enduring example of hachnasat orchim, the mitzvah of welcoming guests.

On Tuesday, Israelis went to the polls to elect their next Knesset, and they did so in extraordinary numbers. More than 5.6 million citizens cast ballots, and turnout reached nearly 78 percent, which is the highest level in more than a quarter century and seven points above the last election in 2022. After years of war, grief, and national trauma, Israelis answered with the most powerful statement a free people can make: they showed up. With nearly all the votes counted, no bloc has secured a majority, and forming a new government will likely take weeks. That uncertainty is not a sign of weakness, because it is exactly how a vigorous parliamentary democracy is supposed to work.

We should not take that for granted. In a region where free and contested elections remain rare, Israel once again held a campaign in which every question was open to debate, the press covered it relentlessly, and the outcome was decided by the voters rather than by any ruler. The rhetoric was often sharp, and at times it crossed lines it should not have crossed. Even so, the ballots were cast, the votes are being counted, and the result will be respected through the institutions Israelis have built together.

One of the most striking stories of this election is the participation of Israel’s Arab citizens. More than a million Arab Israelis were eligible to vote. By most estimates, about three in four of them cast ballots, up from roughly half four years ago, and Arab parties are on track to win about 19 seats, the most in Israel’s history.

Arab citizens campaigned openly, organized in their communities, and elected representatives who will sit in the Knesset and may help decide who forms the next government. Those who cast the Apartheid libel on Israel cannot explain a country in which a minority community votes in record numbers, sends its largest delegation ever to parliament, and holds real political power. Israel is not perfect, and its Arab citizens continue to raise real concerns about equality and opportunity, but they raise them as voters, as legislators, and as full participants in a democracy. That is the opposite of apartheid.

What strikes me is how directly Vayera speaks to this moment. In the very same chapter where Abraham opens his tent to strangers, he also stands before God and argues on behalf of the people of Sodom, pressing repeatedly for justice and mercy. The Torah presents both moments as parts of the same man, which suggests that Abraham did not see hospitality and argument as opposites. He could hold firm convictions and voice them boldly while keeping his tent open to whoever approached. Jewish tradition calls this machloket l’shem shamayim, disagreement for the sake of heaven, and Israel’s lively and often noisy democracy is one of its truest modern expressions.

I believe this offers a meaningful way to think about the role of the Aaron Family JCC in our community. A J is more than a fitness center, a preschool, a summer camp, or a place to attend a program. These are important parts of what we do, but they are also the means through which something larger happens. Every day, people who hold very different views about Israel, about politics, and about Jewish life walk through our doors, sit beside one another at a program, cheer for their children at the same game, and share a table at a holiday celebration. In those moments, the J becomes a tent where differences do not disappear, but where they are held within a shared sense of belonging.

That responsibility extends beyond our building and beyond the people who hold a J membership, because the J is part of the larger fabric of Jewish life in Dallas. At a time when so much of life can feel fragmented and polarized, creating spaces where people can disagree with respect and remain in community is not a small contribution but an essential one. It is also how we stand with Israel: by knowing its story, telling the truth about it, and modeling here at home the same democratic spirit Israelis demonstrated this week.

Abraham’s example reminds us that a community like this does not happen by accident. It is built through intentional acts of hospitality and a willingness to see each person as someone worth knowing, especially when we disagree with them. At the J, that might mean greeting someone who is new, listening carefully to a neighbor whose perspective differs from our own, or making sure that everyone who walks through our doors feels there is a place for them here. These actions may seem ordinary, yet Jewish community has always been built through ordinary moments that carry extraordinary meaning.

In the weeks ahead, as Israel’s leaders work to form a new government, I hope we will take pride in what Israelis accomplished this week and remember the example Abraham sets in this week’s portion. The future of the Jewish people, in Israel and in Dallas, will be shaped not only by the outcomes of elections or the institutions we build, but by the relationships we nurture and the doors we choose to open.

May Abraham’s example inspire us to keep building a Dallas Jewish community, and a Jewish people, where there is always room for one more.

Todd

title: Shan's Spark: Worth The Hype? - Taking a GLP-1. Don't Forget to Lift.
author: Shan Charles
body:
GLP-1 medications have helped many people take an important step toward improving their health. As weight begins to come off, however, many people find themselves asking a new question: 

"How should I be exercising while taking a GLP-1?" 

The answer may surprise you. Many people assume they should increase cardio and try to burn as many calories as possible. While walking and cardiovascular exercise are certainly beneficial, one of the most important forms of exercise during weight loss is strength training. 

Why Strength Training Matters 

When we lose weight, we hope to lose body fat. Unfortunately, the body can also lose muscle along the way. 

Muscle plays a vital role in supporting metabolism, strength, balance, mobility, and healthy aging. Preserving muscle while losing weight can help you maintain your energy, stay active, and support long term success. 

How Often Should You Train? 

For most individuals, strength training two to four days per week is an excellent place to start. Focus on squatting and standing, pushing, pulling, lifting, and carrying movements. 

Don't Underestimate Walking 

Walking supports cardiovascular health, helps increase daily activity, aids recovery from workouts, and can be performed by nearly anyone regardless of fitness level. 

Rest Is Part of the Workout 

If you are lifting challenging weights while taking a GLP-1, do not be afraid to slow down between sets. Allowing 90 seconds to 3 minutes of rest between sets can help you maintain strength, improve workout quality, and approach each set with better focus and energy. 

Remember: strength training is not cardio. The objective is not to get tired. The objective is to challenge your muscles effectively. 

Consider Time Under Tension Training 

Another effective strategy while taking a GLP-1 is a training method known as Time Under Tension (TUT). Rather than simply moving a weight from point A to point B, TUT 

focuses on slowing down the movement and keeping the muscle working for a longer period of time. 

For example, instead of performing a squat as quickly as possible, you might spend three seconds lowering yourself, pause briefly at the bottom, and then stand back up under control. 

The slower and more intentional the movement, the more opportunity your muscles have to do the work. Combined with adequate rest periods, TUT can be an excellent way to support strength, maintain muscle, and maximize the effectiveness of your workouts. 

More Is Not Always Better 

Because many individuals on GLP-1 medications are eating fewer calories, recovery becomes increasingly important. Focus on consistent strength training, regular movement, quality sleep, and proper hydration. 

Fuel Your Muscles 

Prioritizing protein throughout the day can help support muscle maintenance and recovery from exercise. Aim to include a quality source of protein with each meal and snack whenever possible. 

Focus on More Than the Scale 

Ask yourself: Am I getting stronger? Do I have more energy? Is it easier to climb stairs? Am I improving my balance and mobility? These victories often tell a much bigger story than the number on the scale. 

We're Here to Help 

Through strength training, body composition assessments, InBody scans, and personalized fitness consultations, we can help you build healthy habits designed to last far beyond any single phase of your wellness journey. 

The goal is not simply to lose weight. The goal is to become stronger, healthier, and more capable along the way.

title: Shan's Spark: Worth The Hype? - How Strong Is Your Grip?
author: Shan Charles
body:
How Strong Is Your Grip?

Did you know we have a Grip Strength Tester right here at the J? 

Before you click the link below to schedule your complimentary fitness consultation, take a moment to learn why this simple test matters. 

Over the years, I've been fascinated by the connection between grip strength and overall health. What researchers have discovered is remarkable: grip strength is one of the strongest indicators of healthy aging, physical function, and longevity. Studies have shown that lower grip strength is associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease, physical decline, and premature mortality. 

The reason is simple. Grip strength doesn't just measure your hands. It reflects the health of your muscles, nervous system, and overall physical resilience. Dr. Peter Attia, a leading voice in longevity medicine, describes grip strength as one of the strongest physical associations with a longer life. 

Simple Ways to Improve Grip Strength 

  • Squeeze a tennis ball, stress ball, or rolled up pair of socks 
  • Crumple a sheet of paper using one hand 
  • Pinch clothespins open and closed 
  • Hold a coffee mug or water bottle by the handle for 20 to 30 seconds 
  • Practice opening and closing jar lids 
  • Knead therapy putty, modeling clay, or bread dough 
  • Use a hand gripper while watching television 
  • Carry a light bag for short distances around the house 

For those with arthritis or limited hand function, even gentle squeezing and pinching exercises can help maintain hand strength and dexterity over time. Stronger grip strength supports everyday tasks such as opening containers, carrying items, getting up from a chair, and maintaining independence as we age. 

Turn Data Into Action 

When you complete your Grip Strength Assessment at the J, you'll receive a baseline score that you can track over time. Better yet, you can take those results to your physician along with a body composition analysis from our state of the art InBody machine, also available here at the J. 

Together, these measurements can provide valuable insight into muscle mass, body composition, functional strength, and overall wellness. They can help facilitate meaningful conversations with your healthcare provider and support a more proactive approach to your health. 

At the J, we strive to be more than a fitness center. We want to be a trusted ally in your health and wellness journey by providing tools, education, and professional guidance that empower you to make informed decisions about your well-being.

title: Lech Letha: Building in the Desert, Building in Dallas
author: Todd Polikoff, Chief Executive Officer, Aaron Family JCC
body:
I landed back in Dallas this week after nine days in Israel with JCC CEOs from across North America, as part of the JCC Association Kivunim seminar. I am still a little jet lagged, and I am still thinking about what I saw and heard. So, it feels right to me that this Shabbat we read Lech Lecha.

The parsha opens with God telling Abraham to leave his land, his birthplace, and his father’s house, and to go to “the land that I will show you.” Abraham gets no map and no timeline; he gets a direction and a promise that he will be a blessing. Rashi reads the words lech lecha as “go for yourself,” meaning the going is for Abraham’s own good. He must leave home to become who he is meant to be.

I have been to Israel many times, but every trip asks something new of me. This time, the segment of my visit that has been repeating in my head was a visit to Sde Boker, the small kibbutz in the Negev where David Ben Gurion chose to live after he stepped down as prime minister. The home he shared with his wife, Paula, is modest: a simple bed, a desk, and shelves full of books. The man who declared the State of Israel could have lived anywhere, and he chose the desert. He believed the future of the country was in the Negev, so he moved there and helped build it with his own hands.Standing in that small house again, I felt the weight of that choice in a new way.

There is a detail later in the parsha that I love. After Abraham travels down to Egypt, he comes back “to the place where his tent had been at the beginning.” He returns home, but he returns changed, and he builds an altar there. The point of going was what he brought back.

Here is what I brought back for our J community. Ben Gurion looked at the Negev and saw a place to build. He believed a community grows when people show up and do the work, even when the ground is hard. That is what happens at the J every day, in our classrooms, our pool, our camp, and our programs for every age.

I also brought back a picture of how full life is in Israel right now. The cafes were busy, the streets were loud, and families were out together, living fully after everything the country has been through. That resilience is a choice Israelis make every day. They are determined to do more than survive; they intend to thrive, and you can feel it everywhere you go. I see that same energy when I walk through our building: the early morning crowd in the fitness center, our preschoolers on their way to Shabbat, the older adults who have been coming here for decades, and our dedicated staff who make room for all of it.

Ben Gurion built in the desert. Abraham came home and built an altar. Here in Dallas, we keep building, every single day.

‍

Shabbat Shalom,

Todd

title: A Stone of Memory, A Promise from Dallas
author: Todd Polikoff, Chief Executive Officer, Aaron Family JCC
body:
I am in Israel this week at the invitation of the JCC Association, traveling with a small group of JCC CEOs. We are here to explore Israel’s innovation and resilience, grapple with complexity and hope, and deepen our understanding of what it means to lead Jewish communities in relationship with Israel.

Before I left last week, on the morning of October 7, our staff gathered to remember the lives lost and to reflect on what that day still asks of us. As part of the ceremony, we spoke about the Jewish tradition of laying a stone at a grave. I mentioned that I would be visiting the site of the Nova massacre during my time in Israel. Before we left, the team gave me a rock inscribed with the words, “Aaron Family JCC of Dallas, May their memories be for a blessing,” and asked me to leave it at the Nova site.

I carried that rock with me to Israel and, on behalf of our community, brought it to the site of the Nova Festival, where so many young people gathered on October 7, 2023, for music and friendship, never imagining what was coming.

The rock itself is unremarkable. It is not precious or polished, but it carried a community thousands of miles away, one that wants the families, survivors, and people of Israel to know they are not alone.

Jews have long left stones at places of remembrance. Unlike flowers, stones do not wilt; they remain. They are a quiet way of saying that someone came, someone paused, and someone remembered. A stone does not need to be special; its meaning comes from the person who leaves it and the intention behind it.

Standing at the memorial, I looked at the photographs and names that mark the site. Each face was a life, a family, a circle of friends, and a future that should have unfolded differently. These young people had come to celebrate being alive and being together. On October 7, that celebration became a scene of terror, and their futures were taken from them.

When I set our rock down, I was leaving the name of our J in a place of unimaginable loss. Our staff could have written only a simple message of solidarity. Instead, they paired our name with one of the most enduring expressions in Jewish tradition. That inscription says we remember these young people. It says their lives matter to people in Dallas who never knew them and who will not let them be forgotten.

We cannot restore the futures that were stolen, nor can we undo the pain their families carry. But “May their memories be for a blessing” asks something of us. Memory becomes a blessing when it moves us to act, deepens our compassion, strengthens our commitment to Jewish life, and keeps us from taking community for granted. It becomes a blessing when we keep gathering, celebrating, and learning together, even when the world gives us reasons to pull away from one another.

That is part of the work of a Jewish Community Center. We talk a lot about programs, memberships, classrooms, and camps because those are the practical parts of what we do. Underneath them is a larger purpose: making a place where Jewish life is lived and passed on, where our children learn who they are, and where people know they belong. That work does not stop at our building. It connects us to Jews in Israel and around the world, to the people we remember, and to the people we stand up for, even when they are far away.

The rock will stay at the Nova memorial with our name on it. The responsibility it represents comes home with me, and it belongs to all of us. It will show up in how we welcome one another, care for our neighbors, teach our children, and keep Jewish life in Dallas visible and unafraid.

May the memories of those who died be for a blessing, and may that blessing be reflected in everything we do.

title: BBYO and Aaron Family JCC Expand Longstanding Partnership To Strengthen Jewish Teen Engagement In Dallas
body:
Dallas, Texas — BBYO’s North Texas Oklahoma (NTO) region and the Aaron Family Jewish Community Center of Dallas (The J) are proud to announce an expanded partnership designed to deepen Jewish teen engagement and leadership opportunities across the Dallas community beginning in the 2026-2027 school year.

For decades, NTO and The J have worked together to create meaningful experiences for Jewish teens. This renewed collaboration builds upon that strong foundation, reinforcing a shared commitment to empowering the next generation of Jewish leaders through community connection, leadership development, and enriching teen experiences.

“BBYO has given me a place where I’ve been able to grow as a leader, meet some of my closest friends, and feel more connected to the Jewish community,” said Gabe Weisblatt, member of BBYO’s North Texas Oklahoma Region. “Having organizations like BBYO and The J working together creates even more opportunities for teens like me to feel supported, included, and excited to be involved.”

As part of the collaboration, BBYO will continue operating within The J campus while expanding opportunities for co-hosted programming, teen leadership initiatives, and community engagement efforts throughout the year. The partnership will support enhanced collaboration between staff teams, shared promotional efforts, and increased opportunities for teens to engage with both organizations through leadership experiences, events, internships, and community programs.

The expanded partnership reflects both organizations shared vision of creating accessible, welcoming spaces where Jewish teens can thrive and develop a strong sense of identity and belonging.

“The Aaron Family JCC is proud to continue our longstanding relationship with BBYO and invest in the future of Jewish teen life in Dallas,” said Todd Polikoff, CEO of the Aaron Family JCC. “This collaboration represents the power of community partnerships and our collective commitment to ensuring Jewish teens feel connected, supported, and inspired.” This collaboration also reflects the multigenerational impact of both organizations, with many families in the Dallas Jewish community connected to BBYO and the J across generations.

About BBYO

BBYO is the leading pluralistic Jewish teen movement aspiring to involve more Jewish teens in meaningful Jewish experiences. For more than 100 years, BBYO’s purpose has been to unleash the power of youth. BBYO’s leadership programs, the Aleph Zadik Aleph (AZA, high school fraternity) and the B’nai B’rith Girls (BBG, high school sorority), provide exceptional leadership programs and identity enrichment experiences, shaping the confidence and character of hundreds of thousands of alumni who are prominent figures in business, politics, academia, the arts, and Jewish communal life. Together, AZA and BBG form a global Jewish teen movement spanning more than 60 countries. With year-round activities in hundreds of local communities, summer leadership programs, and worldwide travel experiences, BBYO enables teens to explore leadership, service, civic engagement, Israeli education, and Jewish values. Learn more at BBYO. (Please note that BBYO should not be referred to as the B’nai B’rith Youth Organization, but rather as “BBYO.”)

About The Aaron Family Jewish Community Center of Dallas (JCC)

The Aaron Family JCC of Dallas harnesses Jewish values to educate, enrich, and inspire people of all ages and backgrounds so they can become the best version of themselves. Learn more at https://www.jccdallas.org.

title: Three Years After October 7: Showing Up, Loudly, Together
author: Todd Polikoff, Chief Executive Officer, Aaron Family JCC
body:
Dear JCC Family,

On October 7, we will mark three years since Hamas terrorists murdered 1,200 people in Israel, the deadliest single day for the Jewish people since the Holocaust. Three years since families were torn apart, since 251 hostages were dragged into tunnels, since a wound opened in the heart of our people that has not closed and may never fully close. I do not need to recount the details to this community. Too many of us know someone who knows someone, and too many of us felt it in our own bodies before we understood it in our minds.

I have thought a lot about what to say to our community this year. In the first two years, our task was to grieve, to hold each other, to make sense of the senseless. That work is not finished; grief does not run on a calendar, but three years in, I want to talk about something else too: what we do with it.

Let me start with what has stung the most. Since October 7, many of us have felt a particular kind of disappointment, watching people we thought would understand say too little, too late, or nothing at all. We have watched public figures, cultural institutions, universities, and corporations respond loudly to nearly every form of hatred while responding to antisemitism with far less urgency, sometimes with silence. I have felt that gap myself, in conversations with neighbors, colleagues, and people I once counted as allies.

But three years into this, I keep coming back to a different question than “Why are they not showing up for us?” The question I would rather ask is: are we showing up for one another?

I have watched this community prove true again and again since October 7, 2023; the answer to those who want us erased is not to make ourselves smaller. It is to make ourselves louder and prouder, more visibly and joyfully Jewish than we have ever been, and to show up for each other without waiting for anyone else’s permission.

That might sound counterintuitive, because the assumed instinct in the face of hatred is often to duck, to take off the necklace, skip the event, keep your head down until it passes. I understand that instinct, and I have felt it too, but then I think about what those who planned October 7 wanted. They wanted us afraid, hidden, for Jewish life in the diaspora to shrink, and Jewish life in Israel to disappear. Every time we gather, be it at the J or elsewhere in the community for Shabbat, for a preschool sing-along, for pickleball, for a class, for nothing more urgent than meeting a friend, we hand them a defeat.

Visibility matters, but it is not enough by itself. Jewish communities have always been remarkably good at building institutions: schools, synagogues, Federations, camps, museums, and JCCs. We did not build these because we expected the wider culture to make room for Jewish life. We built them because community requires intention, and that lesson matters as much today as it ever has. We cannot force a public figure to speak out or manufacture empathy from an institution that does not feel it. What we can do, what the Aaron Family JCC of Dallas has always done, is build something strong enough that our sense of belonging does not depend on anyone else’s validation.

That is the deeper purpose behind everything that happens inside our walls. A child in our preschool is learning that Jewish values are part of everyday life. A teenage counselor at Camp Chai is finding peers who share the same questions and traditions. A senior in one of our programs is maintaining friendship, purpose, and connection. A parent dropping off a child is building a support network without even realizing it. Sometimes someone walks through our doors needing something no registration form can capture: the simple knowledge that they are not alone.

Every time you walk through the doors of the J or any other Jewish community space, you make a small investment in this community. A membership renewed, a volunteer shift, a Shabbat program, a conversation in the lobby that runs longer than you planned. These moments feel ordinary; they are far from it. They build the relationships that carry a community through hard years, and antisemitism thrives in isolation. When people feel connected instead of alone, they have others to process hard news with, to challenge misinformation with, and to stand beside when it counts.

So here is what I am asking of you, plainly. Do not shrink. Come to the J, or other Jewish space, this week. Bring your kids, wear the Star of David where people can see it, sign up for the class you have been putting off, join the committee. If your membership has lapsed, renew it before the anniversary arrives. Grieve what needs to be grieved; we will always make space for that too, but please do not let grief be the only reason you walk through the doors this year.

Bring a friend who has not been back in a while. Show up on October 7 itself and show up again the week after. We do not need everyone outside of the Jewish community, and our allies, to understand us. We do need you here, showing up for the person standing next to you.

They wanted us gone; prove them wrong. Walk through our doors, and keep walking through them, loudly, together.

title: This Shabbat the Last Word is Us
author: Todd Polikoff, Chief Executive Officer, Aaron Family JCC
body:
Dear J Dallas Community,

This weekend we celebrate Simchat Torah, one of my favorite moments in the Jewish calendar. We read the final word of the Torah, Yisrael, “The people of Israel,” and without pause we roll the scroll all the way back and begin again with the first word, Bereshit, “In the beginning.”

I have always loved that the Torah's last word is not a place, an idea, or a commandment; it is the people.

After thousands of years of stories, laws, journeys, arguments, triumphs and disappointments, the Torah ends with the people who carry it forward. Judaism has always been about who we are together and what we owe one another. That feels especially true right now, when it is so easy to focus on what divides us. We belong to a people and a story that began long before any of us arrived and will continue long after us.

Then we begin again, but not by putting the Torah back on the shelf. We turn it around and start reading. Every generation gets to meet the story fresh and every child who learns a Hebrew word, every family that celebrates a holiday, and every friendship that starts at the J becomes part of it.

That is why community matters so much.

It is easy to gather for a holiday or a big event, but the real work of community happens on the days in between. It happens on an ordinary Tuesday when parents bring their kids to a program, when friends meet at the J, when someone takes a class, works out, volunteers, or sits with someone who needs a friend. More profoundly, it happens when someone simply walks through our doors and knows they belong.

The J is one of the places where Yisrael becomes real. It is where Jewish life moves from an idea into relationships, where generations meet, and where children find out that being Jewish is something you live.

This weekend we will dance with the Torah, hold it close, and start again. The Torah ends with Yisrael and goes straight back to Bereshit. The story belongs to us now, and it is ours to hand to whoever comes next.

I hope you will find time to be with your community this weekend, and in all the ordinary weeks that follow. Every time we come together, we add a little more to that story.

Chag Sameach

title: Shan's Spark: Lift Heavier. Live Stronger.
author: Shan Charles
body:
Lifting Heavier, Not Just Lifting Heavy

As we get older, we often hear the advice: "Lift heavy." While the intention is good, I think there's a better approach: Focus on lifting heavier, not simply lifting heavy.

There is a difference.

Lifting heavily/heavier implies that everyone should aim for a certain amount of weight. Lifting heavier means gradually becoming stronger than you were last month. If your joints feel good, you're eating enough protein, and you're recovering well, adding a little more weight over time can be one of the best things you do for your long-term health.

No matter your age, strength gains, muscle growth, fat loss, bone health, and overall wellness are heavily influenced by three things:

  • Progressive strength training
  • Adequate protein
  • Quality sleep

If your goal is to age gracefully, live a healthy life with purpose, and continue showing up for the people you love, here are my top three tips:

1. Understand the Lifts You're Doing

Don't rely solely on social media for fitness advice. Ask a professional or someone who has trained consistently for years and has a healthy relationship with fitness. Ask them what exercises were hardest to learn, which ones they once disliked, and why they still do them today. Often, the exercises we avoid become some of the most beneficial.

2. Stop Comparing Yourself

Stop trying to look like you did twenty years ago. And stop comparing your progress to someone else's. Everyone's body, history, and circumstances are different. The only comparison that really matters is whether you're making healthier choices than you were before. As the saying goes, comparison is a thief of joy.

3. Prioritize Protein and Sleep

Want to lift heavier? Start by focusing on recovery. Protein provides the building blocks your body needs to repair and grow. Sleep gives your body the time to do that work. Think of protein and healthy foods as the materials for building a house. Sleep is construction time. If either is missing, the final product won't be as strong as it could be.

Shan’s Final Thought

Aging well isn't about proving how much weight you can lift. It's about maintaining and improving your strength so you can continue living the life you want. Instead of asking, ‘How heavy should I lift?’ ask yourself: ‘Am I stronger than I was last month?’ If the answer is yes, you're moving in the right direction. Keep lifting heavier, taking care of your body, and investing in your future self.

‍

At The J, we are committed to being your resource for all things fitness and wellness. Step-by-step, we are continuing to build a brand and an experience that meets you where you are and helps you grow.

Remember, “Change Happens When Change Happens.”

title: A Message for Yom Kippur: No One Atones Alone
author: Todd Polikoff, Chief Executive Officer, Aaron Family JCC
body:
Dear Aaron Family JCC Community,

‍

There's a strange detail in the Yom Kippur liturgy that most of us say every year without noticing.

The Vidui, our confession, is written entirely in the plural. Ashamnu, Bagadnu, Gazalnu. We have sinned, we have betrayed, we have stolen. Not I, we.

You could be standing alone in synagogue, having never stolen anything in your life, and you still beat your chest and confess to theft. Judaism does not let us confess our way through Yom Kippur in the first-person singular. It insists, structurally, grammatically, that atonement is a communal act, not a private one.

That has always struck me as one of the most radical ideas in our tradition: Kol Yisrael Arevim Zeh BaZeh, all of Israel is responsible for one another. On the holiest day of the year, when the stakes are our own souls, Judaism still will not let us stand alone.

I think about that a great deal in this work.

Every day at the J, someone walks through our doors carrying something we cannot see. A senior who has not had a real conversation since Tuesday. A parent quietly unraveling under the weight of a difficult diagnosis. A member who just lost a loved one and does not yet know how to say the words out loud. Yom Kippur asks us to confess in the plural because none of us are actually managing our lives in isolation, no matter how convincingly we perform otherwise. We are carrying each other, whether we notice it or not.

That is not incidental to what a JCC is. It is close to the whole point.

This Yom Kippur, as you fast, reflect, and stand before God with your community, I would ask you to hold two things at once. First, the deeply personal work of cheshbon hanefesh, the honest accounting of who you were this year and who you intend to become. And second, the recognition that your atonement was never meant to be a solitary project. It was designed, deliberately, to be tied to the person praying next to you, and the one you'll never meet.

That is what this building tries to be, 365 days a year, not just on the holiest one. A place where no one has to carry the weight alone.

On behalf of everyone at the Aaron Family JCC, I wish you and your family an easy and meaningful fast. May you be sealed for a year of health, connection, and the kind of community that shows up before you have to ask.

G'mar Chatimah Tovah.

title: Rooted Together for the New Year
author: Todd Polikoff, Chief Executive Officer, Aaron Family JCC
body:
Dear J Family,

In the mountains of Utah stands an aspen grove called Pando, a Latin word meaning "I spread." It looks like thousands of separate trees. It is actually one organism, a single ancient root system sending up trunks for thousands of years. When one trunk falls, the grove loses nothing. It simply grows another shoot from the same roots, which is how Pando has outlasted ice ages and droughts. I think of Pando often when I consider our Jewish Community Center.

We are not simply a fitness floor, an early childhood program, a camp, or a calendar of classes and programs. Those are the visible trunks. What connects them, quietly and without asking for credit, is the root system beneath: a community bound to one another in ways that rarely appear on a program schedule but are the entire reason the schedule exists. Rosh Hashanah asks us to look honestly at the year behind us and the year ahead. This past year tested our community in ways many of us did not expect and would not have chosen.

Yet what carried us through was not any single program, staff member, or leader. It was the network itself, the countless quiet connections between members who may never have met one another, but who are, in every way that matters, part of the same grove. As we enter 5787, I do not ask you simply to attend a class or renew a membership, though I hope you will do both. I ask you to consider yourself part of something rooted, something that has already proven it can hold weight when weight is placed upon it. Bring a neighbor to a class or program. Introduce yourself to someone at the pool you have nodded to for years but never spoken with.

Show up for someone else's lifecycle event as readily as your own. The roots grow stronger only through use. No single trunk holds up this grove. Every one of us does, together, beneath the surface, where it counts most. On behalf of the entire staff and board of the Aaron Family Jewish Community Center, I wish you and your family a sweet, healthy, and meaningful new year.
‍
Shanah Tovah.

title: The Goodbye That Shows Us What WE Built
author: Todd Polikoff, Chief Executive Officer, Aaron Family JCC
body:
Dear JCC Family,

There are moments in parenting that arrive disguised as logistics: a long drive, a packed car, a desk chair that becomes an urgent matter of self-expression. You tell yourself you are helping her settle in, because tasks are easier than tears. But somewhere between the bedding aisle and the final hug, the truth breaks through: you are standing at the edge of her childhood, watching it turn quietly into her adult life.

This past weekend, I moved my daughter into college for her second year, four years after doing the same for my son. I knew the pride and the ache, and the instinct to stay busy so I would not have to feel it all at once. But this time, something landed differently. For the first time, I felt in a deeply personal way how much a community helps prepare a child to step into her own life, amid boxes everywhere, nervous laughter, and hugs exchanged three times before parting ways.

I have spent thirty years in Jewish communal life speaking about continuity, belonging, and the institutions that hold families through Jewish life. I thought I understood the work. Then I watched my daughter walk away into her sorority house, carrying more than we packed in the car, and I understood it in my bones.

This week we read Parashat Ki Tavo, and this year it landed with a specificity I wasn't expecting. The portion opens with the mitzvah of bikkurim: bringing the first fruits of your harvest to the land, and reciting aloud, in full, the story of how you got there. Not just "Here is what I grew." The Torah asks us to tell the entire journey: my father was a wandering Aramean, we were enslaved, we cried out, and we were brought to this place. Only then do we place the basket down. I don't think that's incidental. You cannot simply hand over what you've grown. You must narrate the years that made it possible, or the moment doesn't mean what it should. That is, I think, exactly what a college drop-off actually is: setting down a basket and finally understanding the whole story that filled it.

College drop-off is not really about drop-off day. It is about suddenly seeing everything that came before it. The young woman standing there with a laundry basket full of shoes did not become herself in that driveway. She became herself over years of ordinary Tuesdays, Shabbat dinners, camp cabins, and youth programs, many of them held by Jewish communal organizations. In that moment, I could see flashes of every age she had ever been, gathered inside the young adult now brave enough to begin again without me beside her.

She learned to swim at camp before she could tie her shoes, and there she learned how to miss home and still be okay, how to make and lose a friend, and forgive. In JCC youth theater and synagogue leadership programs, she learned to use her voice and try again after failing. None of that looked like preparation at the time; it looked like childhood. But Jewish communal organizations have always understood something essential: childhood is formation. A camp bunk, a JCC classroom, a youth group bus, a leadership seminar; these are laboratories for becoming, the sacred and often underappreciated work of Jewish communal life.

Jewish communal organizations do not simply offer programs; we help form people. The early childhood teacher who teaches patience, the camp counselor who helps a homesick child through the night, the youth professional who takes a teenager seriously, all are participating in the long work of raising adults, and at its best, it is character formation.

I have often described the Aaron Family Jewish Community Center as "The Center" of the Jewish community; the place people walk through on their way to deeper connection and leadership. Watching my daughter step deeper into her college life, I felt that personally. The Jewish community had been one of her gathering places, giving her a sense of belonging and an identity sturdy enough to carry with her.

So, to the parents dropping off children at college this month, I see you standing in parking lots, pretending to check your phones. I see you in the campus hotel lobby and waiting at the gate for the flight home. To the Jewish professionals, educators, clergy, donors, and communal leaders who helped shape these young adults: I see you too. Your work mattered, in ways hard to measure and impossible to replace.

When I said goodbye to my daughter, I was not only letting go of more of my child. I was remembering the toddler in the pool, the camper with a duffel bag bigger than she was, the teenager finding her voice, the young woman now ready to make a life of her own. I was sending forward the adult that a whole Jewish community helped form. That does not make the goodbye easy, but it does make it holy.

So, parents, travel home safely, call them on Tuesday, not Monday; give them Monday, even if every instinct tells you to reach for the phone sooner. Then come back to the J, the synagogue, the camp, the organization that helped raise them, with gratitude for what this work means. More children are becoming adults every day, and they will need the same gift we received: a community that believes in them before they know how to believe in themselves.

title: Still Here: What the Arch of Titus Reminds Us About Jewish Resilience
author: Todd Polikoff, Chief Executive Officer, Aaron Family JCC
body:
Nearly two thousand years ago, Roman soldiers erected an arch in the heart of their capital to commemorate the destruction of the Second Temple. Carved into its stone is a procession of captured treasures, most famously the menorah, carried through the streets of Rome as a trophy of Jewish defeat. The Arch of Titus was built to declare an ending. It was meant to be the final word on the Jewish people, a monument to our disappearance from history.

Rome, of course, no longer rules anything. The empire that commissioned that arch to mark our destruction exists now only in textbooks and tourist guides. The menorah, meanwhile, was chosen decades ago as the emblem of the modern State of Israel and stands today outside the Knesset in Jerusalem. The people that arch declared conquered are still here, still building schools, still raising children, still gathering in Jewish community centers across the world, including our J in Dallas.

I stood in front of that arch myself during a recent trip to Rome, and I will admit it affected me more than I expected. I have seen photographs of it for years, but standing beneath the carved image of our menorah being carried off as plunder was a different experience entirely. I found myself thinking not only about the ancient world, but about the world we are living in right now, one in which antisemitism is rising in ways many of us did not expect to confront again in our lifetimes. On campuses, in city streets, across social media, and in acts of violence far too close to home, the oldest hatred has resurfaced in new forms while carrying the same old intent. Standing there in the Roman sun, looking up at a monument built to celebrate our destruction, I did not feel despair. I felt something closer to defiance, because I was standing there, in the present tense, and the empire that built that arch was not.

History offers us a lesson if we look closely enough. Every empire, ideology, and movement that has set out to erase the Jewish people has failed, and failed completely, while the Jewish people endured. Not because the threats were not real or the losses not devastating, but because Jewish communities have always understood something their adversaries did not: survival requires building institutions, not simply enduring hardship. The arch that was meant to mark our end has instead become, through the strange irony of history, a monument to our persistence.

This is the work of the Aaron Family JCC, and I do not say that lightly. Every family that walks through our doors, every child in our preschool, every senior in our programming, every member who renews out of commitment rather than habit is part of the same continuity that has carried this people through Rome, through every empire since, and through every wave of hatred that has risen against us. In a moment when so much can feel uncertain, this building and this community remain something solid to stand on.

I do not offer this as comfort alone. I offer it as a call to action. The strength of this community depends on all of us choosing, again and again, to show up, to invest, and to build. That is what has always outlasted the arches built to mark our end.

title: Parshat Ekiev: The Quiet Acts That Carry Us Forward
author: Todd Polikoff, Chief Executive Officer, Aaron Family JCC
body:
Some of the most sacred parts of our lives are the ones we barely notice. This week’s Torah portion, Eikev, opens with an unusual word choice. Eikev means “because,” but it also means “heel,” the part of the body furthest from our attention and yet the part that carries us forward with every step.  

Rashi hears in this a gentle reminder from Moses: do not overlook what seems ordinary, humble, or quiet. The mitzvot we are most likely to take lightly may be the very ones that hold us up.

That image feels especially fitting for a JCC.  

Our community is built not only through big events or milestone moments, but through the small, generous acts that make people feel seen and welcomed: a teacher who knows a child’s name, a class that becomes the highlight of someone’s week, a smile at the front desk, or a staff member who notices when a familiar face has been missing. These moments may be quiet, but they are deeply holy.

As we wind down the summer season together, I invite you to notice the heel, not just the headline.

Come to a class.
Introduce yourself to someone new.
Offer your presence, your kindness, or your support when our community calls.

None of these acts may feel momentous alone, but together they become the foundation we stand on, and the blessing through which we carry one another forward.

title: What Moses Knew About Community: Parashat Va'etchanan and the Work of the J
author: Todd Polikoff, Chief Executive Officer, Aaron Family JCC
body:
In Parshat Va’etchanan, Moses has just been told, again, that he will not enter the Land. He has led this people for forty years; through slavery, through revolt, through the golden calf, through the long tedium of the wilderness, and the answer is still no. He does not retreat into grief. Instead, he teaches. That choice is the entire parshat in miniature, and it is the case for why a Jewish Community Center matters.

The Handoff Is the Point

Parashat Va'etchanan contains the Shema and the Ve'ahavta, the closest thing Judaism has to a mission statement. Read past the famous lines and the actual instructions appear: “V'shinantam l'vanecha,” teach them diligently to your children. Speak of them at home and away when you lie down and when you rise up. Bind them, write them, post them where you will see them constantly.

This is not abstract piety. It is a design brief for how a people transmits itself. Moses is not the point. The chain is the point, and a chain holds only if every link is built; not inherited by accident, but built, generation after generation, in rooms where people show up.

That is a J's mandate, whether or not the institution has ever put it in those terms. We are in the business of “V'shinantam,” of ensuring Jewish life and Jewish belonging are built into the next generation of Dallas, not merely discussed with fondness by the generation before it.

Remembering Sinai So You Do Not Forget Who You Are

Moses later turns to memory as a survival strategy: guard your soul diligently, lest you forget the things your eyes have seen; the fire, the voice, the whole community gathered as one at Horeb. He is not asking Israel to remember a historical fact. He is asking them to remember what it felt like to belong to something larger than themselves, because that feeling will keep them tethered once the wilderness fades into legend and the challenges ahead multiply.

This is the quiet risk facing Jewish communal life today, and Dallas is not exempt. The erosion rarely announces itself. It is a family that stops coming because nothing pulled them back. It is a young professional who never finds their people. It is a child who grows up with no felt experience of communal joy to draw on later, when memory is what he will need most.

A J exists to manufacture Sinai moments on an ordinary Tuesday: at the pool, in a preschool classroom, at a Mahj lesson, in a room of seniors who have shared a weekly card game for a decade. These are not programs offered for their own sake. They are the practice Moses is prescribing.

The Whole Community, Not Just the Congregation

The gathering at Horeb includes everyone: men, women, and children, present together for the covenant. Va'etchanan does not treat Jewish continuity as a project for the already affiliated. It imagines a full tent.

That is the distinct role a J holds, one no other communal institution quite replicates. We are the address for the Jew who will not walk into a synagogue this week but will walk into a fitness center, a summer camp, a cultural arts series, a senior lunch program. Va'etchanan's vision of one people gathered depends on a door wide enough for everyone to walk through. In Dallas, that door is here.

Why This Matters to You

Moses never crossed into the Land he spent his life building toward. He taught anyway. He structured the handoff, insisted on memory, and insisted on gathering, because his task was never to finish the story. It was to ensure the story could continue without him.

Every donor, volunteer, and board member who invests in this J does the same work. None will personally witness the full arc of what they are building: the child in our early childhood center who becomes a lifelong Jewish communal leader, the isolated senior who finds a second family at lunch, the interfaith couple who finds their way into Jewish life because room was made for them. We build it anyway, because Va'etchanan is direct on this point: the handoff is not optional, and it does not happen by accident.

It happens because a community decides, deliberately and repeatedly, to teach, to gather, and to remember, together. They do it at the J!

title: Devarim: The Story We Choose to Tell
author: Todd Polikoff, Chief Executive Officer, Aaron Family JCC
body:
Dear J Members,

This week we read Parshat Devarim, and with it, Moses begins the last, longest speech of his life. Forty years of history, compressed into one final address to a generation standing at the edge of everything he had worked for.

Buried in that recap is a scene worth further conversation. Moses reminds the people of the spies, the twelve men sent to scout the land, ten of whom came back and said, in effect, it cannot be done. They reported that giants live there, the cities are fortified, and we are grasshoppers next to them. Only two, Caleb and Joshua, looked at the same land, the same giants, the same fortified cities, and said: we can do this.

Here is what strikes me every time I read it: none of the twelve lied about the facts. The giants and the walls were real. The spies were not wrong about what they saw. They were wrong about what it meant.

Ten men looked at a hard thing and concluded it was impossible. Two men looked at the same hard thing and concluded it was worth doing anyway. The difference was not the information; it was the story they chose to tell about it.

The story of the spies often comes to mind for me in the work we do here at the JCC and in the challenges we face. I would guess many in our community have similar challenges, regardless of the room they sit in, the board they serve on, or the business or family challenge in front of them right now. Almost nothing we take on as a community is easy.

‍

‍Building, growing, sustaining Jewish life in Dallas has never been the "Small hill" version of the job.

‍

There are always giants: cost, capacity, competing priorities, a world that feels less certain than it did a decade ago. Those things are real, and I am not going to be the one to tell you they are not.

But the Torah does not let the ten spies off the hook for seeing giants. It holds them accountable for what they did with that sight, for the fear they spread, for the story that turned a hard truth into a reason to stay put. Caleb's response was not blind optimism. He had seen the same giants. He simply refused to let the size of the obstacle write the ending before anyone had tried.

That's the muscle I want us to build together as a community: the ability to see clearly and still move forward. Not denial or naive positivity, just the discipline to look at something difficult and ask,

‍

"What would it take," instead of stating that, “We can’t."

‍

It is also, not coincidentally, the same discipline this moment in the Jewish calendar asks of us. Devarim is always read on the Shabbat before Tisha B'Av, the day we remember what happens when a community loses its nerve and, later, when it loses itself entirely. The rabbis draw a direct line from the sin of the spies to the destruction that followed centuries later. A people that talks itself out of the land it was promised is, in some sense, the same people that talk itself into believing it is not worth defending. The stakes of the story we tell ourselves are not small.

So, as we move through the next few weeks leading up to Tisha B'Av, I would ask you to notice the story you are telling yourself about whatever giant is currently standing in your way. Whether it is here at the J, in your business, or at your kitchen table.

The land does not get smaller because you called it impossible. It just stays unclaimed.

I look forward to seeing you at The J!

Shabbat Shalom.
